content:
The mist clung to the valleys of Mount Lu like damp silk, silencing the cries of the night birds. Below the peak, in a bamboo-walled study, Scholar Wei sat with his brush poised over mulberry paper. The ink on his stone slab had long since dried, yet he remained motionless, staring out at the garden where the moon cast long, skeletal shadows across the moss.

It was the season of the Hungry Ghosts, when the veil between the quick and the dead is thinnest. Wei, a man of logic and classical texts, did not believe in such superstitions. He believed in order, in the hierarchy of the Emperor, and in the clarity of the written word.

But tonight, the silence felt heavy, as if the air itself were holding its breath.

A soft scraping sound, like dry leaves skittering across stone, drew his attention to the veranda.

"Who goes there?" Wei called out, his voice steady. "The hour is late for visitors."

There was no answer, only the shifting of the bamboo curtain. A woman stepped into the study. She wore robes of deep cerulean silk, the color of twilight, but they seemed faintly translucent, shimmering with a quality that defied the lantern’s yellow glow. Her hair was bound in a simple jade hairpin, and her face was pale—the color of old parchment.

She did not walk; she drifted, her feet silent against the polished floor.

"Forgive the intrusion," she said. Her voice was like the rustle of wind through dry grass. "I have come seeking a scribe. My own hands… they have become clumsy with dust."

Wei frowned. "It is unseemly for a woman to be wandering alone at this hour. Where is your household? What do you seek to have written?"

She glided closer. The lantern flame flickered violently, though the windows were shuttered. She placed a small, polished inkstone on his desk. It was carved from black jade, ancient and freezing to the touch.

"A letter," she whispered. "To be delivered to the Magistrate in the city of Wuzhou."

Wei reached for his brush, his curiosity piqued despite his skepticism. "State your grievance, then."

She dictated, and Wei began to scribe. The ink flowed thick and dark, smelling faintly of decay and wet earth. The words were not of courtly grievances or tax disputes. They were a lamentation of a life interrupted—of a carriage overturned in the ravine by the temple ruins, of a secret wedding interrupted by floodwaters, and of a promise made beneath a weeping willow that was never kept.

As Wei wrote, he felt a profound cold seep into his bones, numbing his fingers. He looked up to ask a question, but his words died in his throat.

The woman was gone.

Yet, a draft remained. On the desk, the paper he had been writing upon was now perfectly dry, as if the ink had aged not minutes, but centuries. He looked down at the characters he had inscribed. They were no longer in his own elegant hand; they were jagged, desperate, and terrifyingly precise.

Beneath the last line, there was a red smudge—a thumbprint in dried blood.

Shivering, Wei gathered his courage and took a lantern to the veranda. The garden was still, the bamboo swaying rhythmically. He walked to the edge of the property, where a stone path led into the deep woods. Just beyond the gate, half-buried in the tall grass where a decorative lantern had fallen years ago, he found it: a small, splintered piece of wood from a carriage wheel, twisted and scorched by lightning.

Beside it lay a ribbon of cerulean silk, perfectly clean, as if laid there moments ago.

The next morning, Wei traveled to the city of Wuzhou. He sought the Magistrate, a man of advanced years, and presented the letter.

The Magistrate’s face went white as he read. His hands trembled so violently that he dropped the scroll. "Where did you find this?" he rasped, clutching the silk ribbon Wei had brought. "This was the favor I gave to my betrothed before the carriage fell into the ravine forty years ago. Her body was never recovered."

Wei did not speak of the woman in his study. He did not tell the Magistrate of the freezing air or the smell of wet earth. He simply bowed, leaving the Magistrate to weep over the words he had been waiting four decades to hear.

That night, back on Mount Lu, Scholar Wei sat at his desk. He did not light the lamp. He sat in the darkness, watching the mist dance. He knew he would never truly be alone again, for in the silence of the mountains, he could hear the faint, scratching sound of a brush against paper, writing a thank-you note that would never find a post.
